en: The *Kādambarīsvīkaraṇasūtramañjarī* [states]:

"In the seven-threaded sacrifice performed by the Self-born (Brahmā), the consumption of *vāruṇī* (wine) is shown as being absolutely necessary for the acceptance of non-alcoholic liquor (*anutarṣa*), because it serves as the means for that sacrifice and is the cause for the arousal of ineffable bliss.

[* Now, he demonstrates the drinking of *vāruṇī* as a means for that [sacrifice], or as the cause for the arousal of ineffable bliss, within the seven-threaded sacrifice being performed by the Self-born. *1* [ *] "In the seven-threaded sacrifice performed by the Self-born... etc. [he says].
The term *anutṛṣ* means "to quench thirst" or "to obtain ineffable bliss"; that by which this occurs is *anutṛṣa*, namely *kādambara*. Its acceptance is its consumption (*anuprāśana*).

The extreme necessity of that consumption—that is, its being the most desired object—arises because it bestows ineffable bliss and acts as an aphrodisiac. For these reasons, the meaning is that the acceptance of Pracetas’s daughter must be performed prior to the performance of the ritual. 1.2
"‘Makaradhvaja’ and ‘Ātmabhū’ [are names for Kāma], according to Amara [Kośa] 1.3.

‘Saptatantu’, ‘Makha’, and ‘Kratu’ [are names for sacrifice], according to Amara [Kośa] 1.4. Now, does the acceptance of thirst assist in the awakening of an unseen result (*adṛṣṭaphala*), or rather in the awakening of a seen result (*dṛṣṭaphala*)?"

Having presented the doubt-provoking statement, "or is it something that assists [the means of knowledge]," and having resolved in his mind that only the awakening of a perceived result directly assists [the means of knowledge], whereas no Vedic (ānuśravika) statement— such as those concerning results like heaven— can be postulated as an assisting factor, he teaches the second sūtra as the reason for the preceding sūtra. [1.5]
Because it serves as the cause for the awakening of the bliss of passion (*ratyānanda*), which is an ineffable bliss.
[Regarding "of the bliss of passion":
it should be understood as occurring when the acceptance of insatiable longing has been accomplished.]

By this statement, the causal relationship between these two is established; and thus the meaning is as follows: when the acceptance of mutual longing has been performed, an inexpressible bliss of passion (*ratyānanda*) arises during the act of sexual union, and not otherwise; for just as in the case of substances such as soup and vegetables unmixed with salt, a taste that is neither flavorless nor sweet manifests—this is the sense. (2.3)
Furthermore, another indefinable benefit is taught and demonstrated by the third sūtra.
[2.4] In the rising from the *udañji* posture, there is the state of being the supreme cause for the acceptance of a wise maiden.
[3] Regarding the phrase "in the rising from the *udañji*": [3.1]

The meaning is as follows: when the son of Pāśin has been brought to a state of identity with his own wife through the intensification of extreme affection, that [union]—by virtue of being an extremely helpful instrumental cause (*nimittakāraṇa*)—becomes the means (*prayojaka*) for his own bliss to result in an inexpressible joy. By this statement, having first performed such an immersion (*nirveśana*) of that kind because of its absolute necessity, [he performs it] prior to that [subsequent union].

The meaning is that one possesses authority over the performance of the ritual (*karmādhikāra*) through the sevenfold thread (*saptatantu*); otherwise, due to the failure of the power of enthusiasm (*utsāhaśakti*) regarding the instrumental cause (*nimittakāraṇa*), there occurs a total destruction of the ritual activity (*narmavyāpāra*). [3.3] He shows the definitive conclusion (*rāddhāntasūtra*) for this aphorism. [3.4]

Because it is impossible to prescribe the system of sexual union (*ratitantra*) in the absence of the status of being the primary agent belonging to the one being acted upon (*prayojya*). [Regarding the phrase "in the primacy of the one being acted upon" (4.1): When there is rising up, the status of being the primary agent belongs to the one being acted upon (*prayojya*, i.e., the woman). In its absence—that is, in the absence of rising up—by the principle that when the cause ceases, the effect also ceases, [the aforementioned status does not exist].

Why would the *ratitantra* (the system of sexual union) be lost? (4.2) Because of the absence of its efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*). Just as the production of the effect, a cloth, occurs when the shuttle, loom, and other tools are present, but not otherwise; so too, the production of the ritual procedure of the *tantra* occurs when there is sexual arousal (*abhyutthāna*). (4.3) By this statement, the sense is that having first ensured the acceptance of the drink through its absolute necessity, one should then proceed to the act of lovemaking. (4.4)

Now, having summarized the entire purport of these four sūtras in their totality, he demonstrates the unerring definitive statement (*rāddhāntavākya*) for all the sūtras: [4.5] "Because there is no authority to perform the system of sexual union (*ratitantra*)—which is characterized by activity involving all limbs—when the object of pleasure (*prayojya*) is engaged in an extensive play of dalliance (*narmavyāpāra*) and the woman (*udañji*) is distinguished by her rising up. [5.1] "'When the object of pleasure is engaged in an extensive play of dalliance'..."

In the preceding sūtra, whatever degree of authority was defined by way of limitation within the external tantra (*bāhyatantra*), in this sūtra, however, when the complete absence of the motivating cause for engaging in play occurs, the absolute non-existence of even the activity of the one being motivated is established; thus, a certain specific prescription is attained through mere lack of resolve.

The sense is that [the object] is not perceived there. 5.2 * Therefore, immediately following the acceptance of the absence of thirst (*anuttarṣa*), there is the state of being qualified for the office of ministerial service (*narmakarmādhikāra*); this is the single intended meaning of the five sūtras. 5.3 * This is a restatement of the very doctrine established in the *Māgha*, *Kirātārjunīya*, and *Raghuvamśa*; it should not be suspected that it was spoken by inventing a novel injunction based on one's own imagination. 5.4
Furthermore, for a person who has passed beyond the second stage and is united with his wife— who, by good fortune, manifests a love previously unacquainted—

and who experiences the arising of various flavors [of pleasure], the collection of fermented liquor (*sīdhu*) is not considered the supreme cause, because such a mental disposition is absent; however, in other circumstances, it is the very cause for the manifestation of an ineffable bliss from the impurity of food.

Acceptance through appropriation is indeed intended as being of the utmost necessity; having conceived a knowledge of reality through such consciousness, one must accept with intense longing the qualification for such action. Thus, he instructs in accordance with a true teaching, like the words of a trustworthy person, for those engaged in the practice of play. [5.5]
In the *Ratitantravilāsa*, regarding the production of an inexpressible aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), the collection of *sīdhu* liquor is the supreme cause.
(6) [Regarding the phrase "in the *Ratitantravilāsa*":
in the *Ratitantravilāsa*, which is an elegant treatise on amorous activities, concerning the production of an inexpressible *rasa* that transcends the sixfold [classical] *rasas*...]

The meaning is this: that essence which is fit for the enjoyment of those who feed on nectar—that is to say, the supreme cause of tasting the flavor of *kādambara*—when such an essence has been drunk, it generates an awakening of ineffable bliss in those skilled in the particular cultivation of aesthetic flavor (*rasa-bhāvanā*) during the expansion of the activities of sexual union. 6.2
Furthermore, he demonstrates another indescribable variety of flavor through the tasting of *sīdhu* liquor:
[6.3] "The natural disposition of the daughter of the Lord of Puṣkara consists in the graceful arrangement of amorous dalliance.
[7] ["Graceful arrangement of amorous dalliance" (lalitavibhramabandha): 7.1]
"Pushkara is [the lotus] facing in all directions," according to Amara.
(7.2) The meaning of the aphorism is that it is the natural disposition of the daughter of the Lord of Pushkara to manifest graceful and playful movements.
(7.3) Here, by the term "Lord of Pushkara," the lord of the western quarter is indicated; [it refers to] his daughter.

When the consumption of the Vāruṇī [wine] is performed, it serves as the cause for manifesting graceful and playful gestures; otherwise, since the entirety of literature possesses a divine nature, compositions that delight the inner organ even without effort emerge from the lotus-face of the consumer,
like the emergence of a lotus from the region of the netherworld (atala).
The meaning is that they manifest.

This very distinct excellence of aesthetic flavor (*rasaviśeṣāntara*) becomes the instrumental cause for the accomplishment of the supreme transcendental result (*paramāpūrva*) by way of the principle of "auxiliary assistance through conjunction" (*saṃnipatyopakārakanyāya*).
It serves as an inexpressible means for the awakening of the god of love (*manasija*) through the mere hearing of the fixed phonemes (*nirbandhavarṇa*), by means of that [awakening].
This alone is its ultimate cause; this is its innate nature.
(7.5) Furthermore, another distinct benefit is demonstrated by the subsequent sūtra:
(7.6) "Together with the appearance of the dawn, it acts as the prompter for the boldness of the rising flow of honey. (8)
"Let her be near," [it is said].

She who exists in proximity (*upa*) to the state of being dark (*śyāmā*) is "near-dark" (*upaśyāmā*). With that woman, who consists of fourteen or fifteen years of age, the drinking of honey-mead (*madhuvāra*)—the practice of drinking honey—is the cause for upward-turning boldness (*udañcid-dhārṣṭya*), that is, for extreme firmness.
By this statement, the essential nature of the restrictive injunction (*parisaṃkhyā-vidhi*) is revealed.
Thus, the meaning is as follows: when the honey-moon festival (*madhuvāra*) occurs together with a woman who has passed her prime, audacity (*audārya*) does not arise toward her;
likewise, any such resolve becomes futile, according to the maxim of pouring water into an overturned jar.

Therefore, the meaning is that a wise man, even if he possesses boldness in the playful arts of love (*ratitantravilāsa*), should never engage in a honeyed dalliance with a woman whose youth has faded;
for according to the maxim, "no one's mind ever turns toward a futile exertion. (8.3–8.4)
Following the opinion of Dhanvantari and others, he demonstrates another benefit in the consumption of *kāpiśāyana*, which manifests an ineffable joy:
[8.5] "Enjoyment with Śyāmā for a period of two watches (*yāma*)—marked by the desired limit—is the supreme cause for the retention of semen.
[9] "[With Śyāmā]" [9.1].
It is well known in the *Vātsyāyana-sūtra* that a woman of sixteen years is "dark-complexioned" (*śyāmā*).

In the verse, "The women entered into dalliance with a woman in such a state, drank, and experienced intoxication," the word *nirveśana* indicates drinking. The suffix *-dvayasac* is used in the sense of measure according to the rule *pramāṇe dvayasac*, [forming] *yāma-dvayasam*; thus, it refers to that which is characterized by such a measure [of time].
Since the *Kośa* records that "time" (*kāla*) means both "appointed time" and "duration," the phrase "for that long" means for as long as it takes to arrest the emission of semen.

This is the meaning: when the consumption of wine together with her is performed, it acts as the supreme cause for arresting the semen, such that for the duration of one watch (*yāma*), it strikes the generative organ like the pounding of rice grains. 9.2.

Now, regarding the expansion of amorous activities, he demonstrates that the consumption of *kāpiśāyana* wine before sexual union is absolutely necessary for one who has not yet experienced the joy and bliss of amorous pleasure, as it serves to dispel the exhaustion of lovemaking;
this is because the drinking of wine is extremely essential when the hairless vulva is joined with the penis.
[10] [Regarding the phrase "when the hairless vulva is joined with the penis": 10.1]

That from which body hair has emerged is "nisthanūruha," meaning devoid of the appearance of body hair; that which is both such and a "varāṅga" (the private organ)—its "sambhedana" (piercing) is the tearing open of its mouth by one's own *udañji* [tongue]. When such an act is being performed, one who is unaware of the playful intent (*narmavyāpāra*) should be made to consume *aireya* [wine]; once the *aireya* has been consumed, there arises the pain of the torn abode of the mind-born [god of love].

It is not experienced at the time of separation; otherwise, due to the pain arising from the house being torn asunder, the *vyāna* wind undergoes a displacement within the channels (*nāḍī*) situated in the house, and an extreme distress of constriction is experienced. To ward off that pain, the meaning is that one should have [the woman] drink two *palas* of *kāpiśāyana* wine prior to sexual union. // 10.2
When that woman had drunk the Kāpiśāyana wine, she demonstrates by means of the subsequent verse the pleasure arising from drinking:
"While the after-drinking is being performed, the pain of the piercing is not felt. (11) ["While the after-drinking is being performed" means: (11.1)

It should be understood that this occurs when the tasting [of the fruit] is performed through the mediation of a dear friend; the meaning is that because there is no conscious awareness due to the onset of intoxication, the pain arising from the piercing is not experienced.
(11.2) [In the following day, he points out another benefit:
On the following day, the private organ appears as if unpierced. (12) [End of section]
"On the following day" (12.1).

Immediately after the opening of the vulva (*varāṅga*), on the following day, this very vulva appears as if unopened or unrent; this is another benefit. (12.2) By means of the woman's consumption [of the seed], he demonstrates the excellence of the fruit in the form of a subsequent [result]. (12.3)

While the amorous activity is being performed, the fruit-bearingness of the audacity of the penis (*udañji*) is observed. (13) [Commentary: Regarding the phrase "while the amorous activity is being performed": when the amorous activity—in the form of a reply—is being carried out as sexual intercourse, the "fruit-bearingness" refers to the male organ (*meḍhra*), which has attained an extreme hardness like a wooden staff due to the audacity of the penis (*udañji*). It is "fruit-bearing" because it produces the fruit of pleasure. *Udañji* is derived from the root *añj* with the prefix *ud-* and the suffix *-in*, meaning "that which causes erection. The term *phalegrahi* is a *karmadhāraya* compound formed by adding the suffix *-in* to the word *phala* according to Pāṇini 3.2.26 (*phalegrahir ātmambhariś ca*). This suffix is applied to denote the agent who performs the action expressed by the verbal root, provided that the action results in the production of the fruit (*phala*). Thus, it means "one who bears fruit" (*phalaṃ gṛhṇāti*). The suffix *-in* is added to the word *phala* to signify the fruit itself, and the resulting form is *phalegrahi*. The masculine gender is used here because it refers to the male organ. Alternatively, one might argue that since the word *udañji* is feminine, the word *phalegrahi* should also be feminine. However, this is not a fault; for even though the word *udañji* is feminine, the word *meḍhra* (penis), which is its substantive, is masculine. The efficacy [of the wine] is seen to be unfailing.

This is what is meant: by the mere consumption of the Kāpiśāyana wine, even the most tightly contracted vulva of a woman lacks the capacity to burst open the mouth of the most rigid penis, and thus it meets with defeat.
The meaning is that [the pleasure] is indeed attained.

(13.3) Even when the female organ has been moistened by the consumption of *kāpiśāyana* wine, a great pain arises in the two labia (*udañjau*) as they open the aperture of the woman's organ which had reached a state of extreme contraction;
by this statement, the intended sense is that even in the second stage, the man experiences a pleasure that was previously unburst forth. (13.5)

[13.6] It has been taught that the arousal of the pleasure of passion, the stabilization of virility (*vīryastambhana*), and the duration of time [occur] during dalliance with Śyāmā in the bedchamber; furthermore, it prescribes the practice of consuming *aireya* as being absolutely essential even when engaged in play with Upaśyāmā.
[14] When the *vyānata* and other postures are employed with Upaśyāmā, the consumption of the daughter of Pāśin is the cause—the instrumental factor—for the experience of ineffable bliss.
"With Upaśyāmā" (14.1).
When the intellect is present in an external practice with those who have not yet reached full youth, one should administer [the substance] to her in a minute amount;

for by that much alone, both will experience the bliss of joy (*ānanda-sukha*). While the activities of kissing and so forth are being performed, [the result occurs] through the mere slight internalization [of the substance].
Because the experience of bliss is observed there, those bound by fetters do not possess it in excess.
[14.2] Keeping in mind the causal argument that "the acceptance of one's own daughter" is the reason, he teaches the subsequent aphorism:
[14.3] Because the purpose is fulfilled by consuming even a minute amount during sexual union with girls who have not yet reached puberty. [15]
"Together with those who have not yet attained youth" (verse 16).

[Now, regarding the consumption of *aireya* during the stage of full youth, it is taught in the *Ratitantravilāsa* that this is for that specific state and not for other stages, considering that there is no utility or eligibility in other states; thus, its absolute necessity in the second stage is demonstrated by the following Eastern Sūtra. 16.1.

When there is a combination with the preceding form (*pūrvarūpa-saṃyoga*), the acceptance of the *ka* suffix is absolutely necessary in the state that constitutes the base (*prakṛti*) for the *tīya* suffix.
[Regarding "in the state that constitutes the base for the *tīya* suffix":
this refers to the second stage, where [the form] is *dve tīya*.]
From this [word] "dvi," when the suffix *tīya* is applied, the word *dvitīya* is formed. It should be understood that at that stage, there is an absolute necessity for acceptance;
that is, it occurs when there is a combination of the previous form (*pūrvarūpa*) and when such a woman is in close proximity.
17.2 *Objection:* Is the acceptance prescribed with a visible purpose in view, or with an unseen result (*adṛṣṭaphala*) in view? [Answer: Because here, only a visible purpose is required.

It is not for the sake of some unseen purpose; rather, it is for a seen purpose. For the firmness of the *udañji* (the upward-turned lip) is a precursor [to sexual union], and its seen purpose is the manifestation of an extreme abundance of *usrā* (vitality/sexual vigor) in the facial and chest regions. For the sake of experiencing these three fruits, a man who has reached the second stage must, as an absolute necessity during the time of amorous play, take up the *sīdhu* (wine) together with the woman.
The meaning is that it must be performed in every way.

[17.3] However, he says that when the third case-ending is in its original state (*prakṛti*) as distinguished by *saṃprasāraṇa*, it is not absolutely necessary. [17.4] But in other states, there is no status as a governing factor (*adhikāraka*). [18]
"In other states" (taditarāvasthāyām) [means]:
in the state occupied by a betrothed maiden and in the state of one who has not yet reached puberty, he has no entitlement to its consumption.
He demonstrates two sūtras as the reasons for both cases.
Because of the absence of complete knowledge in one case. (19) [Regarding "because of the absence of complete knowledge in one case":

in one instance, for a person who has reached the stage of youth (*paugaṇḍavayas*) and is approaching manhood, at a later time when the period of life has been equalized by the presence of disease, there is an absence of the full maturation of the blind essence (*andhas*), the sapid essence (*rasa*), and the seminal essence (*retas*); therefore, in such a state of action, [the result does not follow].]
There is no qualification [for that], because in the other case, the constituent parts consisting of the five elements are even more diminished.
Regarding the phrase "in the other case": [it refers to the other realm].

Even in the state of old age, because it was observed that all the functions of the senses had become extremely diminished in their own activity due to excessive engagement in amorous play with the daughter of Diṣṭa at that time, the intended meaning of the two sūtras is that neither the child nor the aged man has the qualification for the performance of amorous acts. (20.3) By the principle that "when the limiting adjunct in the form of the cause exists, there is the manifestation of the limiting adjunct in the form of the effect," through the grace of Padmā—

[20.4] He demonstrates the conclusion of the section: it is far more appropriate that those who have attained the status of universal monarchs and the like should follow this path of the Flower-Bowed One (Kāmadeva) at all times, as a constant duty like a regular ritual obligation, and not others.
[21*] For people who are dear to Hari, following this branch [of dharma] is absolutely essential.
"Of those people who are dear to Hari.

(21.1) Now, if it is asked, "In the case of a single injunction, where is the prohibitive statement enjoined?"—it is said with the intention that it applies to those who are the counter-correlates (*pratiyogin*) of the aforementioned people: (21.2) "For others than those, engagement in this scripture is not enjoined. (22)

"Of others than that" (taditareṣām) means those who are devoid of the power of the daughter of the Milky Ocean (Kṣīrodajā). [Objection: If one asks, "Where is such an injunction for action found to be universally applicable due to its extreme necessity? [the author] demonstrates that locus.
By the principle of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), this treatise applies to those joined with the daughter of the ocean. [Regarding "by the principle of elimination":
the state of being a remainder is *pāriśeṣya*; therefore, by means of that which is devoid of both negation and pervasion, it applies to those conjoined with the daughter of the ocean.]
Thus, the meaning is that the operation of the scripture concerning the acceptance of lying down proceeds for the sake of awakening to an ineffable bliss. [23.2] He points out another opinion:
[23.3] Mārkaṇḍeya and others maintain that the acceptance of insatiable thirst (*anutarṣa*) on the day of the lunar eclipse (*ghasra*) is absolutely necessary. [24]
Regarding the phrase "on the day of the offspring of the lineage" (*gotrāpatyaghasreṣu*):
the son of Mṛkaṇḍu holds the view that it refers to the day (*ghasram*) of the offspring (*apatyam*) of the lineage (*gotrāyāḥ*), and on that day, there is the taking of food (*anutarṣasvīkaraṇam*).
He shows the opinion of those others in the following sūtra.
On the days of Kāvya, this is most essential for Suratha and Vaiśya.
(25) [Regarding "on the days of Kāvya":
According to the lexicon, Śukra, the preceptor of the Daityas, is called Kāvya; and according to Amara, *ghasra* means day or *ahar*. (25.1–25.2)
* "Suratha and others"—by the word "others," the Vaiśya is included.
[25.3] He demonstrates the intended meaning of the injunction regarding the restrictive rule:
[25.4] because the two statements are applied to those who possess the practice of the powers (*śakti*). [26]
For others than those, there is instruction according to the time.
[Regarding the two sentences:
this rule—that the practice must continue for two days—applies only to those who possess the capacity for worship; for people other than them...]
For those who follow the system of Pralambaghna, however, there is instruction according to the specific time; thus, the meaning is that there is no restriction to two days.
Furthermore: in the second caste, permission is granted for all times. 28. [27.2–27.3] * What more? 27.3] In the second caste, there is authorization for all times. 28 [27.4]
Regarding the phrase "in the second caste" (dvitīyavarṇe):

[28.1] In the second caste, that of the Kṣatriyas, the rule for the consumption of Kāpiśāyana wine is intended as a constant duty for those of a tamasic nature who possess the qualification for worship, consisting of the continuous consumption of Kādambara liquor. [28.3] Since the body of the Self-born (Brahmā) is the material cause when one perceives his true nature through direct experience, it does not follow the two days of the week like those possessing the qualification for worship.
[28.4] It establishes a restrictive rule for the color prescribed by instruction.
[29] By means of the sacrifice, there is permission for the first color according to the scriptural text.
[29.1] "By means of the sacrifice" means:

By the two statements, "In the Vājapeya, he takes the cups of surā" and "In the Sautrāmaṇī, he takes the cups of surā," there is an authoritative injunction for the first caste (the Brāhmaṇa) regarding both the taking and the drinking of the cups exactly as prescribed by the text.

(29.2) Thus, the meaning is this: in the Vājapeya, however, only the taking of the cups is permitted; the permission to drink belongs only to the third caste (the Vaiśya). Accordingly, the scriptural statement [of the Veda] says: "They cause a conflict."
Regarding the term "vājasṛt":

in the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice, the consumption [of the offering] is prescribed by the Vedic formula for the performer of the sacrifice alone, and not for the other officiating priests (*ṛtvij*). Furthermore, there is another opinion that even in that case, the act of consumption is accomplished merely by smelling [the substance];
such is the statement of other sages.

[29.5] He concludes the meaning of the section: "The permission for [the consumption of liquor] at all times applies only to the lords of the [six] flavors (*rasādhipatayaḥ*), and not to other people.
[30] "Even for those people who possess the splendor of sovereignty over a region (*khaṇḍamaṇḍalādhipatya*) and so forth, the indulgence (*vilāsa*) in taking *sīdhu* [liquor] is for all times.
[30.1] "[Regarding the phrase] 'sovereignty over a region and so forth'..."

The meaning is that for kings who rule over small territories, whose subjects are satisfied by their benevolence toward the world, the experience of luxury through the consumption of liquor is not a constant indulgence; rather, it is practiced in accordance with the opinions of Suratha, Vaiśya, and others. 30.2
[30.3] He demonstrates the rule regarding the consumption of young women.
[31] Permission for young women [to eat] by virtue of their association with one's own beloved.
[31.1] "By virtue of their association with one's own beloved."

The permission to consume *kādambara* is granted only at the time of sexual union with one's own husbands, and not in any other state; for what purpose would it serve otherwise? Since its consumption would be a fruitless effort in such cases, even within this restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*), a further specific distinction is attached: therein too, the rule applies only during the *ananyaja* sacrifices and not elsewhere. [31.3] Therein also, it is prescribed only for the *ananyaja* sacrifices and not in other instances. [32]

*In that case as well, it is only during sacrifices performed by those of non-twice-born origin (ananyaja) [that this applies]. (32.1) The rule for accepting liquor (anuttarṣa) out of absolute necessity applies only during sacrifices performed by those of non-twice-born origin, and not at other times outside of that.* (32.2) Here, by the inclusion of the term "woman" (yoṣā), only those such as Upaśyāmā and others are included, and not women whose second state [of marriage] has been lost.
Having determined that consuming from the lotus-mouth of a woman yields a distinct and most excellent fruit, he demonstrates its consumption as being of absolute necessity.
(32.3) Consuming from the lotus-mouth of a woman is the unfailing cause for the awakening of speech. (33) *
"By means of the lotus-mouth of the woman":
(33.1) the meaning is that when the consumption [of the nectar] is performed by means of the lotus-mouth of the woman, there occurs a spontaneous manifestation of speech according to one's desire.
(33.2) By this statement, the meaning is that even for a person devoid of the effort of hearing and so forth, the speech of the gods manifests from their own mouths without any exertion. (33.3)
[33.4] He further demonstrates another superior distinction of fruit, merely by way of acceptance:
[34] the tasting from the thousand-petaled lotus of Śyāmā’s mouth, which is the direct perception of the nature of the primal source (mūlaprakṛti).
[34.1] “From the thousand-petaled lotus of Śyāmā’s mouth.”

The tasting of the lotus flower from Śyāmā is the direct cause for the immediate perception of the true nature of the primordial material cause (mūlaprakṛti). When the tasting is performed with her, one comes into union with the primordial material cause, which is the cause of the entire phenomenal world. 34.2
* Or rather, the meaning is that one perceives its true nature directly, without mediation.

(34.3) * By this statement, the meaning is that one also attains fruits such as union (*sāyujya*) without effort. (34.4) * At the time of sexual union, the drinking of wine should be performed as enjoined by the ritual rule. (34.5)
That description of amorous play, which was previously taught in the Kāmaśāstra,
should all be performed for the sake of obtaining pleasure from the woman,
for the sake of experiencing one's own pleasure as well, and for the purpose of producing offspring. (34.6–34.8)
"He obtains two fruits: offspring and likewise the pleasure of desire.
At the time of his end, that man attains the world of Urvaśī.

Thus ends the *Kādambarasvīkaraṇasūtra*, together with its commentary—a work composed by the illustrious and preeminent royal sage Purūravas for the amusement of lovers, forming an integral part of the playful arts of love.
